study.title: Genesis 18 The Lord's visit, the promise to Sarah, and the intercession by Sodom
study.overview: Genesis 18 shows two central movements: first, the LORD visits Abraham and renews the promise of the son through Sarah; then he reveals to Abraham the judgment against Sodom and leads him to intercede with reverence and boldness. The chapter highlights Abraham's hospitality, God's faithfulness to the promised time, the seriousness of collective sin, and the righteousness of the Judge of all the earth. It also shows that the prayer of intercession is born of trust in the righteous and merciful character of God, not of an attempt to force him to change will.

outline.title: The visit received with honor
outline.explanation: The LORD appears to Abraham in the oaks of Mamre, and Abraham runs to receive him with humility and generosity. The text emphasizes its readiness to serve: water, rest, bread, meat, milk and butter. The scene contrasts with the corruption that will appear in Sodom and presents Abraham as someone attentive to his neighbor and willing to serve with plenty.

outline.title: The promise to Sarah and the revelation of judgment
outline.explanation: Visitors ask for Sara and announce that she will have a child in the appointed time by God. Sarah laughs in his interior, and the Lord corrects her unbelief with a decisive question: nothing is difficult for God. Then the group goes toward Sodom, and God declares that he will not hide from Abraham what he will do, because Abraham was chosen to form a house that keeps the way of the LORD, practicing righteousness and judgment. The cry of Sodom is great, and sin is described as very serious.

outline.title: The intercession of Abraham by Sodom
outline.explanation: Abraham abides before the LORD and comes near to intercede. He appeals to God's righteous character and asks whether the righteous would be destroyed with the ungodly. The conversation progresses in five steps, from fifty to ten righteous, showing the patience of God and the persistent humility of Abraham. The chapter ends with the LORD leaving and Abraham returning to his place, after praying with reverence and courage.

study.context: The chapter fits into Abraham's journey already established in the previous promises. The text itself links the visit to the confirmation of Isaac's birth, and the comments provided treat her as a moment of intimate revelation in which God speaks as a friend and also as a judge. There is no need here to resort to historical reconstructions beyond what the text and notes affirm: the scene takes place in the tent of Abraham, in the oaks of Manre, and the narrative prepares the immediate contrast with Sodoma, which will be developed in the next chapter.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God is at the same time near and holy. He accepts Abraham's hospitality, promises to fulfill what he has spoken, and at the same time judges sin with righteousness. The question about Sarah points out that divine power is not limited by age, sterility or human impossibility. The phrase on the way of the Lord shows that Abraham's election is not only privilege, but a responsibility: his house must teach justice and judgment. In intercession, Abraham does not argue for self-interest; he prays for others and appeals to the character of God himself. The narrative suggests that biblical prayer does not deny divine sovereignty, but relies on it, recognizing that the Judge of the whole earth acts straightly.

scholarViews.insight: The Lord's visit to Abraham anticipates the fulfillment of Isaac's promise of the birth and shows fellowship with God as something associated with a shared meal.
Abraham approaches God in prayer with holy concern and reverence, using the revelation received to intercede for Sodom.
Upon reaching ten righteous, Abraham to insist, showing that he thought that there was unlikely to be less than that in the city and that he continued as the divine presence remained with him.

questions: What does Abraham's hospitality teach about serving God through service to others?
Why do the question about Sarah, and God's answer, confront our tendency to measure divine action by human experience?
How does Abraham's intercession correct a prayer centered only on personal needs?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to unite hospitality, faith and prayer. In practice, this means welcoming people with real generosity, trusting that God can fulfill what seems humanly impossible and intercede for cities, families and people in a situation of sin or vulnerability. It also invites us to examine whether our home and our routine teach justice and judgment, as Abraham's house should teach.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not unanimously explain the exact identity of the three visitors; Tyndale's commentary says that they were probably the LORD and two angels, while other notes only present them as three men or three angels in human form. There is also no basis for notes to determine additional historical details about Manre or the exact chronology of the visit beyond what the text itself and the comments claim.
